records.people: Bank of Papua New Guinea (audited entity); Auditor-General of Papua New Guinea (Auditor General's Office)
records.summary: The Auditor-General of Papua New Guinea's Report Part IV 2024 on the accounts of public authorities and statutory bodies devotes its section 2 to the Bank of Papua New Guinea and records that his report on the Bank's financial statements for the year ended 31 December 2023, issued on 14 October 2024, carried a Qualified Opinion, while the 2024 report carried no qualification. The accompanying audit observations reported to Ministers find discrepancies between general ledger balances and independently computed balances on foreign currency denominated accounts, attributed to control weaknesses including incorrect year-end valuation of foreign investments held with external fund managers, failure to revalue accrued interest receivable at the year-end buy rate, and non-revaluation of derivative assets and liabilities; also that minutes of several committee meetings were not properly recorded or made available for audit, that the month-end process for IMF-related interest charges remained ineffective, that one December 2023/January 2024 FX intervention with a commercial bank deviated from the required settlement sequence, and that a list of prior-year internal control and accounting deficiencies remained unaddressed.
records.detail: The central bank is the subject of the audit, not the auditor: the Auditor-General audits the Bank's accounts and records under sections 8(2) and 8(4) of the Audit Act, and these are his findings against the Bank's own control environment and financial reporting. This is a separate episode from the money-laundering investigation around Elizabeth Genia already on the map for Papua New Guinea, with different years, different documents and no named individuals.
records.quote: The 2023 report contained a Qualified Opinion while 2024 report did not contain any qualification.
records.source_title: Report of the Auditor-General Part IV 2024 on the Accounts of Public Authorities and Statutory Bodies, section 2 'Bank of Papua New Guinea' (pp. 3-7)

records.people: Bank Negara Malaysia foreign exchange dealings (Royal Commission of Inquiry findings; no individual named in this source)
records.summary: The Royal Commission of Inquiry into Malaysia's foreign exchange losses, whose 528-page report was tabled in Parliament on 30 November 2017, concluded that Bank Negara Malaysia incurred losses of about RM31.5 billion on foreign exchange dealings between 1992 and 1994, drawing the figures from the central bank's own internal Accounting Treatment Report, an audit report for 1992, the Auditor-General's letter for 1993 and board minutes for 1994, and found that the losses had a significant negative effect on the national economy and impaired Bank Negara's ability to fulfil its mandated role as the country's central bank.
records.detail: The central bank's own trading losses and the way they were recorded are the subject of the inquiry, so the bank is the body examined rather than the one examining. This is a distinct episode from the two banknote-related bribery records Malaysia already holds (the Securency/NPA note-contract findings of 2001-2003 and the Mohamad Daud Dol Moin prosecution), with different years, different people and a different document. It rests on a national newspaper's report of the tabled inquiry report rather than on the inquiry report itself.
records.source_title: The Star, 'Forex RCI: Bank Negara losses affected Malaysia's economy', 30 November 2017

records.people: State Bank of Pakistan (audited entity); an unnamed Australian national appointed Deputy Governor; eight unnamed senior officers at the SBP Lahore office; Auditor General of Pakistan
records.summary: A press account of the Auditor General of Pakistan's audit for 2022-23 reports that the audit found financial irregularities exceeding Rs243 billion at the State Bank of Pakistan and that the central bank had repeatedly failed to safeguard the national exchequer and the interests of consumers, itemising a Rs105 billion loss from selling securities below their purchase price, a Rs1.96 billion loss on the printing of commemorative Rs75 notes, Rs59 billion of defaulted loans issued by state-owned banks, the appointment of an Australian national as Deputy Governor on an annual salary of Rs120 million which the audit called a violation of regulations, and Rs63.5 million of medical stock embezzled by officers with no inquiry begun after sixteen months. The Auditor General of Pakistan's own Annual Report 2022-23 was downloaded and does not mention the State Bank, so the sectoral audit report this account describes has not been located and the record rests on the press account alone.
records.detail: The State Bank is the audited entity and the subject of every finding listed, not the body doing the finding. It is a separate episode from the 2025 allegation already on the map that fresh Eid banknotes were diverted by SBP officials to brokers. The source is a specialist trade newspaper reporting the Auditor General's report rather than the report itself: the Auditor General of Pakistan's own Annual Report 2022-23 was downloaded and searched and does not mention the State Bank at all, so the underlying sectoral audit report was not reached. Treat the figures as press-reported until the audit report itself is located. This record does not claim to be the TERF audit that the Public Accounts Committee ordered on 8 August 2023, which the source does not mention.
records.source_title: Customs Today, 'AGP uncovers Rs243b irregularities in SBP'

blanks.note: Royal Audit Authority of Bhutan, Annual Audit Report 2023-24 Volume I (English), downloaded in full (4.25 MB, 255,127 characters of extracted text) and grepped for 'Monetary Authority', 'Central Bank' and 'RMA'. The Royal Monetary Authority appears exactly twice: once in the list of abbreviations, and once at an observation in the significant-findings chapter whose subject is the Bhutan Development Bank Limited, which 'had not capitalized Fixed Equated Instalment Facility account to its primary account after becoming NPL despite directives from the Royal Monetary Authority of Bhutan', with the RAA recommending that the matter be pursued with the RMA. There the RMA is the regulator whose directive was ignored, i.e. the detector, not the subject. Volume I is a consolidated summary of 228 of the 525 audit reports the RAA issued between 1 July 2023 and 30 June 2024, so a per-entity RAA audit report on the RMA may exist and was not reached; a press article, 'Financial watchdog RMA dogged with its own irregularities in RAA report' (thebhutanese.bt), was returned by search and NOT opened for want of budget. That is the single best lead left for Bhutan.

Inversion test run and it closes the audit vein for Hong Kong. Audit Commission of Hong Kong (Director of Audit), Annual Report 2023-24, paragraph 11 and Appendix A read: 86 accounts were audited and certified in 2023-24, namely all of the Government's accounts and those of the Hong Kong Housing Authority, the Exchange Fund, five Trading Funds and 69 other funds, and Appendix A lists all 86 by name. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority is not among them; the only related entry is item (33) 'Exchange Fund', an account the Commission certifies rather than an audit of the HKMA, and the annual report records no finding against it. The Commission's value-for-money reports are a separate series and were not reached.

Two more Vanuatu Ombudsman public reports from the same PacLII series as the 1996 report already on the map were opened in full and neither has the Reserve Bank of Vanuatu as its subject. (1) 'Further Public Report on the US$100,000,000 Bank Guarantees', 22 October 1996 (paclii.org/vu/other/ombudsman/1996/10.html): the findings are against Hon. Barak T. Sope for breach of the Leadership Code; the Reserve Bank appears only as a body that received expert advice and whose Governor was consulted, and no Reserve Bank official is found to have done anything wrong. (2) 'National Bank of Vanuatu Former Board Members' Trip to Fiji', 10 September 1997 (paclii.org/vu/other/ombudsman/1997/4.html): the findings are against five former National Bank of Vanuatu board members and the former General Manager, and the National Bank is a government-owned commercial bank, not the central bank. Note for the next round: paclii.org serves HTML to WebFetch but returns a 5,660-byte Cloudflare 'Attention Required' page to curl, so grep-the-download does not work on this host.

Secondary blank alongside the filed record: the Auditor General of Pakistan's own 'Final Annual Report 2022-23' (agp.gov.pk/SiteImage/Misc/files, 5.08 MB, 113,082 characters of extracted text) was downloaded and grepped case-insensitively for 'State Bank' across the whole document — zero hits. The AGP's annual report is an account of the department's own activity and does not carry entity findings, so the Rs243 billion figure must sit in a separate sectoral or entity audit report that was not located. Two searches of agp.gov.pk returned entity audit reports for the Federal Board of Revenue, ZTBL and social-safety-net programmes but none for the State Bank.

Macao's Comissariado da Auditoria publishes per-subject audit reports through the Legislative Assembly (al.gov.mo attachments) and an annual policy-lines document. The policy-lines document for 2024 (gov.mo/pt/.../2024CA_p.pdf, 73 KB, 19,912 characters) was downloaded and grepped for 'Monet' and 'AMCM' — zero hits, but it is a statement of the Commissariat's own work programme and carries no list of audited entities, so no inversion test was performed and Macao has not actually been tested. The al.gov.mo 'Relatório de Auditoria' attachments returned by search are the per-subject reports and are the place to look; none was opened.

Taiwan was searched twice in Chinese for Control Yuan corrective measures (糾正) and Ministry of Audit special examinations naming 中央銀行, 中央印製廠 or 中央造幣廠. Searches returned Control Yuan gazette and publication PDFs on cy.gov.tw, multimedia.cy.gov.tw and cybsbox.cy.gov.tw, but every one of the four cy.gov.tw PDFs attempted returned an identical 1,161-byte error body to curl rather than the document — nothing was tested. These hosts need WebFetch, or the percent-encoded path, rather than curl with UTF-8 path segments. Explicitly NOT attempted, per the assignment: the Ministry of Audit's consolidated government account, which is not an audit of the bank's own statements.

Solomon Islands searched for a second court case involving a Central Bank of Solomon Islands officer. Candidate judgments at pacliirms.austlii.edu.au (SBHC/2015/86, SBHC/2024/176, and several SBMC PDFs) were identified but the host returned nothing to curl, and no budget remained for WebFetch. Also unread: the Office of the Auditor General's reports on the CBSI. The country has not been tested.

blanks.iso3: AFG, ARE, JOR, KWT, LAO, SYR, THA, TLS, TON, WSM
blanks.note: Ten of the nineteen assigned countries were not reached at all within the fetch budget; the budget went on the audit-series vein in the countries most likely to have a per-entity report (PNG, PAK, BTN, HKG, MYS) plus the Pacific court/ombudsman vein. For each of these ten, their existing have_cases and have_events entries were read so a duplicate check is already done, but no document was opened, so none of them should be recorded as a negative. The standing leads are: Jordan's Audit Bureau (ديوان المحاسبة) annual report; Kuwait's State Audit Bureau reports to the National Assembly; Thailand's State Audit Office annual reports; Timor-Leste's Câmara de Contas; Tonga's Auditor General reports (Tonga already holds two records); Samoa is already a documented negative on this vein in closed_negatives.json and should not be re-run.

checked_not_in_assignment.note: Not in my list and not researched; the assignment records them as already closed by the inversion test or by case-by-case reading of Nazaha statements. Not re-run.

Thought of as a promising audit-series country (BPK publishes per-entity reports on Bank Indonesia) but it is NOT in my assignment, so I looked it up in have_cases.json rather than researching it: Indonesia is present there, so anything found would have been a duplicate risk and no fetch was spent.

leads_not_opened.lead: thebhutanese.bt, 'Financial watchdog RMA dogged with its own irregularities in RAA report'
leads_not_opened.note: Bhutan. Returned by search, not opened. Points to a Royal Audit Authority per-entity audit report on the Royal Monetary Authority, which would be exactly the vein this round is built on. One fetch, high probability.

leads_not_opened.lead: External fund managers named in the PNG audit — NOT my row
leads_not_opened.note: The Auditor-General's 2024 observations on the Bank of Papua New Guinea name 'External Fund Managers (EFM) including Schroders, Lombard, and Black Rock' as holding the Bank's foreign investments, at the point where it finds their year-end valuation was done incorrectly. That is reserve-manager material for the managers row, not a corruption case, so I have not filed it. party_names.json already carries 'Schroder Investment Management', 'BlackRock' and 'BlackRock Investment Management'; 'Lombard' is ambiguous in the source (it carries 'Lombard Odier Asset Management (Europe) Limited' and 'Lombardi Capital', and the audit's bare 'Lombard' does not settle which) and no head office is stated anywhere in the document, so a manager record from this would need null cities. Source: https://ago.gov.pg/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Report_Part-IV-2024.pdf p. 4.

leads_not_opened.lead: Report of the Auditor-General Part IV, PNG, other years
leads_not_opened.note: This is a true annual per-entity series and the Bank of Papua New Guinea is section 2 of every edition. Part IV for 2010, 2012, 2018, 2019 and 2021 are all openly served at ago.gov.pg/wp-content/uploads and were not opened. Each is a separate candidate; the 2024 edition reproduced the 2024 observations and said the 2023 report 'contained similar observations', so earlier years are likely to carry distinct findings.

The 528-page RCI report was tabled in Parliament on 30 November 2017. Parliament's own site (parlimen.gov.my) would carry it and would let the Malaysia record drop weak_source and name the individuals the press reports name (Nor Mohamed Yakcop as responsible, and findings on concealment); not attempted for want of budget.

notes: Fetch accounting: 8 WebSearch calls, 4 WebFetch calls, and 8 curl download attempts (of which 4 failed: two cy.gov.tw PDFs, one paclii batch, one pacliirms batch), so about 20 units against a budget of about 25. No tool reported a rate limit.

Duplicate checks: every one of the 19 assigned countries had its have_cases.json and have_events.json entries read in full before any fetch, and closed_negatives.json['cases_unavailable'] was read for all 19 — only Samoa (WSM) appears there. The three filed records were each checked against the existing records for their country on person, episode and source URL: PNG's existing record is the 2023-2025 Elizabeth Genia money-laundering investigation (occrp.org) and its events are a 2023 search and a 2021 Central Banking Act review, none of which is the Auditor-General's financial-statement audit; Malaysia's existing records are the Securency/NPA note-contract bribery findings (rba.gov.au) and the Mohamad Daud Dol Moin acquittal (theedgemalaysia.com), plus a 1998 resignation-under-pressure event, none of which is the 1992-1994 forex loss inquiry; Pakistan's existing record is the 2025 Eid-notes diversion allegation (pakobserver.net) and its events are a 2014 governor resignation and the 8 August 2023 PAC direction, none of which is the 2022-23 AGP audit.

Four of the nineteen assigned countries (MYS, THA, TON, WSM) already hold two case records each in have_cases.json rather than exactly one, so coverage.py's 'exactly one' count appears to exclude something the file includes (Samoa's second record is flagged counterparty_only, which may explain that one but not Malaysia, Thailand or Tonga). Worth checking before the next depth round picks its list.

Status strings: all three records are filed as 'official finding', which is accurate for each — a supreme-audit-institution finding, a royal-commission finding and (for Pakistan) a reported audit finding. Nothing was flattened onto a nearer label.

No quote field was filled from a WebFetch summary. The only quote in this file, on the PNG record, was copied character-for-character out of pdftotext output of the Auditor-General's own PDF. The Malaysia and Pakistan records have no quote field because the wording I had came back through WebFetch and I could not verify it as the page's own characters.
